Title: The Development of a Machine Learning Model to Predict Daily Wildfire Growth Across the Continental United States
Brief Abstract:
Wildfires burn millions of acres across the United States each year threatening human lives and property. As rapid growth occurs in the wildland-urban interface (WUI), where houses and vegetation meet, wildfires are becoming more of a pressing issue. In addition to WUI growth, climate change continues to result in a warmer and drier climate, promoting increasingly favorable conditions for wildfires. As a result, forecasting and messaging elevated wildfire potential to partners and the public is crucial. Several fire weather indices, such as the Hot-Dry-Windy index developed by Srock et al 2019, have been developed. However, these indices are either tied to a particular topographical region or composed of various different atmospheric or fuel variables. Given the disparity among fire weather indices, a need for a consolidated fire weather prediction model is needed.

In order to consolidate these forecasting indices, a machine learning model has been developed to predict daily wildfire spread across the Continental United States should a fire develop in any given location. The model accounts for 96 different atmospheric, fuel, topographical, special, and static variables such as population density, topographical slope, and regional fire climatology to predict daily wildfire growth. The resulting model shows skill in predicting areas of active fire growth out to three days in the future for new fires across the United States. This work serves as a useful foundation for predicting fire spread across spatial and temporal scales using machine learning in real time. Eventually, ML model output will allow for precise relocation of emergency resources and increase preparedness for the general public ahead of significant fire events, protecting lives and property

Title: Realtime Fire Weather Forecast and Fire Risk Visualization
Brief Abstract: The website, hosted by Texas Tech University's Atmospheric Science Group, provides real-time fire weather forecasts and fire risk visualizations specifically for the southern region. It is associated with the university's efforts in numerical weather prediction and focuses on delivering data-driven insights for fire weather conditions. For inquiries, the site lists contact information for Dr. Brian Ancell (Professor), Mr. Brandon Tomerlin, and Dr. Deepak Kumar, all affiliated with the Department of Geosciences.

Title: Red Flag Threat Index (RFTI) Visualization
Brief Abstract: This interactive web-based tool provides real-time fire weather forecasting and fire risk visualization for the Southern United States and Southern High Plains. It calculates the Red Flag Threat Index (RFTI), a composite metric used to identify critical fire weather conditions by integrating high-resolution meteorological data from the Weather Research and Forecasting (WRF) model and machine-learning (ML) algorithms. The tool visualizes hourly RFTI values and daily fire growth potential, assisting fire managers and meteorologists in identifying areas where wind speeds, relative humidity, and fuel dryness converge to create extreme fire danger.

Title: Sensitivity to the Representation of Wind for Wildfire Rate of Spread: Case Studies with the Community Fire Behavior Model
Brief Abstract: Accurate wildfire spread modeling critically depends on the representation of wind dynamics, which vary with terrain, land cover characteristics, and height above ground. Many fire spread models are often coupled with coarse atmospheric grids that cannot explicitly resolve the vertical variation of wind near flame heights. Rothermel's fire spread model, a widely used parameterization, relies on midflame wind speed to calculate the fire rate of spread. In coupled fire atmosphere models such as the Community Fire Behavior Model (CFBM), users are required to specify the midflame height before running a fire spread simulation. This study evaluates the use of logarithmic interpolation wind adjustment factors (WAF) for improving midflame wind speed estimates, which are critical for the Rothermel model. We compare the fixed wind height approach that is currently used in CFBM with WAF-derived winds for unsheltered and sheltered surface fire spread. For the first time in this context, these simulations are validated against satellite and ground-based observations of fire perimeters. The results show that WAF implementation improves fire perimeter predictions for both grass and canopy fires while reducing the overestimation of fire spread. Moreover, this approach solely depends on the fuel bed depth and estimation of canopy density, enhancing operational efficiency by eliminating the need for users to specify a wind height for simulations.

Title: The Community Fire Behavior model for coupled fire-atmosphere modeling: implementation in the Unified Forecast System
Brief Abstract: There is an increasing need for simulating the evolution of wildland fires. The realism of the simulation increases by accounting for feedbacks between the fire and the atmosphere. These coupled models combine a fire behavior model with a regional numerical weather prediction model and have been used for fire research during the last few decades. This is the case, for instance, for the widely adopted Weather Research and Forecasting model with fire extensions (WRF-Fire). Typically, the coupling includes specific code for the particular models being coupled such as interpolation procedures to exchange variables between the atmospheric grid to the fire grid, and vice versa. However, having a fire modeling framework that can be coupled to different atmospheric models is advantageous to foster collaborations and joint developments. With this aim, we have created, for the first time, a fire behavior model that can be connected to other atmospheric models without the need for developing specific low-level procedures for the particular atmospheric model being used. To this end, the fire behavior model, referred to as the Community Fire Behavior model (CFBM), makes use of the Earth System Modeling Framework (ESMF) library to communicate information between the fire and the atmosphere. More specifically, CFBM is available as a national unified operational prediction capability (NUOPC) component which allows for an agnostic coupling to atmospheric models and other Earth system components. CFBM closely follows WRF-Fire version 4.3.3 methods in its version 0.2.0 which allows us to verify the adequacy of our implementation. The CFBM can be also run offline using an existing WRF simulation to propagate the fires in what we refer to as the standalone model. Herein we describe CFBM and its implementation in the Unified Forecast System (UFS). Simulations of the Cameron Peak Fire performed with UFS and WRF-Fire are presented to compare results from both models in order to verify our implementation. Results from both models, as well as with the standalone version, are consistent indicating a proper development of the CFBM and its coupling to the UFS-Atmosphere. This is the starting point to go beyond WRF-Fire methods and improve the realism of the simulations in the future. The possibility of using the fire behavior model with other atmospheric models provides an attractive collaborative framework to further improve the realism of the CFBM model in order to meet the growing demand for accurate wildland fire simulations.

Title: Community Fire Behavior Model
Brief Abstract: The Community Fire Behavior model simulates the evolution of wildland fires. The model requires the definition of a grid with characterization of the fuels and elevation to simulate the fire evolution. The fire physics of the current version of the model (v0.2.0) is based on the WRF-Fire physics. This has allowed us comparative testing with WRF-Fire to ensure a proper implementation of the model (Jimenez y Munoz et al. 2024).  The Community Fire Behavior model can be run offline, reading external atmospheric data (from WRF at this moment), or online, coupled with an atmospheric component to account for fire-atmosphere interactions.

Title: Fire Behavior Software Documentation
Brief Abstract: This documentation supports a software package designed to model wildfire behavior, including fire spread, intensity, and environmental interactions (e.g., fuel consumption, smoke emissions). Hosted on Read the Docs, it provides user guides, installation instructions, configuration details, and potentially API references for researchers and modelers. The software is relevant for WoFS-Smoke development, as it likely generates inputs like fire emission rates or plume characteristics for smoke forecasting within the Warn-on-Forecast System. While the documentation itself is not a dataset or code, it describes how to use the software, which interfaces with datasets like satellite-derived land surface properties (e.g., MODIS/VIIRS) or fire detection data (e.g., GOES-R). It is a critical resource for configuring and evaluating fire behavior models that feed into smoke prediction systems like WoFS-Smoke.

Title: The Community Fire Behavior Model (CFBM)
Brief Abstract: This webpage serves as the official hub and software portal for the Community Fire Behavior Model (CFBM) developed by the NCAR Research Applications Laboratory. CFBM is designed to simulate the evolution, spread, and behavior of wildland fires. Its underlying fire physics are derived from WRF-Fire, allowing it to operate either offline (driven by external meteorological datasets like WRF) or online (coupled directly to larger earth-system frameworks like the Unified Forecasting System via ESMF/NUOPC to account for two-way fire-atmosphere feedbacks, heat/moisture fluxes, and smoke dispersion). The site links out to its public GitHub repositories, user guides, and implementation documentation.
Principal Investigators: Research Applications Laboratory (RAL) at NSF NCAR (Lead contact: Pedro Jimenez Munoz)

Title: CFBM simulations and verification dataset for sheltered and unsheltered wildland fires
Brief Abstract: This dataset contains simulation and evaluation files for four wildland fires simulated using the Community Fire Behavior Model (CFBM): two unsheltered ground fires (Boone Draw and Murphy) and two sheltered canopy fires (Hayden Pass and Indian Valley). The package includes WRF model driving simulations at 1 km resolution, 100 m GEOGRID domain definitions, CFBM output fire perimeters and fuel types, and observational evaluation data from VIIRS active-fire detections and observed fire perimeters.

Title: Fire simulations of the early phase of the Cameron Peak Fire with UFS-CFBM, WRF-Fire, and offline CFBM
Brief Abstract: This dataset contains fire progression simulations of the early phase of the 2020 Cameron Peak Fire using three modeling approaches: the Unified Forecast System coupled to the Community Fire Behavior Model (UFS-CFBM), WRF-Fire, and standalone offline CFBM. The collection includes coupled (two-way) and uncoupled (one-way) fire-atmosphere simulations initialized across three distinct timeframes, observed fire perimeters used for model evaluation, and idealized fire line propagation benchmark simulations under homogeneous conditions.
